props.title: Manhattan Baby

sections.content: Manhattan Baby (1982) represents Lucio Fulci diving into supernatural horror with Egyptian mysticism, following his gore-soaked classics The Beyond (1981) and City of the Living Dead (1980). The film meshes Fulci's signature eye trauma imagery with an The Exorcist (1973)-inspired possession narrative, though trading Catholic elements for Egyptian mythology. While not reaching the visceral heights of his earlier works, it showcases Fulci's attempt to blend giallo-style kills with a more mainstream supernatural thriller approach.

sections.content: The film's Egyptian connection places it within a specific subset of 1980s Italian horror that drew inspiration from ancient curses and artifacts. Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981) had popularized Egyptian archaeological horror, leading to Italian productions like Demons 2 (1986) incorporating similar elements. Manhattan Baby specifically echoes the "evil artifact affecting children" trope seen in Poltergeist (1982), though with Fulci's distinct European horror sensibilities.

The film's production values reflect the declining Italian horror industry of the early 1980s. While earlier Fulci films like Zombie (1979) had substantial budgets for practical effects, Manhattan Baby relies more heavily on optical effects and atmosphere. Still, cinematographer Guglielmo Mancori, who also shot The Beyond, creates striking compositions that elevate the material beyond typical supernatural thriller fare. sections.content: Manhattan Baby marks a transition point in Italian horror cinema, as filmmakers moved away from the explicit gore of the late 1970s toward more psychological terrors. This shift can be seen in contemporaneous works like Dario Argento's Tenebrae (1982) and Lamberto Bava's A Blade in the Dark (1983), which began incorporating more mainstream thriller elements while maintaining distinctly Italian stylistic flourishes.
